## 1. Research Vision

My research sits at the intersection of signal processing, machine learning, and clinical medicine. The question that organises my work is a practical one: **how do we build diagnostic systems that are not only accurate on benchmark data, but interpretable, verifiable, and deployable in the hospitals and laboratories that actually need them?** In a health system such as Pakistan's, where specialist pathologists are scarce, diagnostic workloads are rising, and cancer is frequently detected late, this question is not academic. It determines whether a model becomes a clinical instrument or remains a figure in a paper.

My trajectory has moved from hardware implementations of signal processing algorithms, through deep learning for biomedical image analysis, to my current programme in computational pathology for prostate cancer. The through-line across all three phases is the same engineering discipline: *a method is only as good as its behaviour under real constraints* — finite precision, finite compute, finite data, and the messy statistical reality of clinical cohorts. I am drawn to problems where the interesting difficulty is not the availability of a model class but the fidelity of the measurement, the honesty of the evaluation, and the feasibility of deployment.

## 2. Foundations: VLSI Implementation of DSP Algorithms

I was trained as an electrical engineer, and my early research concerned the VLSI implementation of digital signal processing algorithms. My published contributions in this area focused on **direct digital frequency synthesis (DDFS)** — the design of hardware-efficient synthesiser architectures in which the phase accumulator, the phase-to-amplitude conversion stage, the quantisation strategy, and lookup-table compression are traded against spectral purity, silicon area, throughput, and power consumption. The central design tension in DDFS is well known and unforgiving: every bit of word length removed from the phase or amplitude path reduces area and increases speed, and every such reduction shows up directly in the output spectrum as spurious content. There is no way to hide an approximation; it becomes measurable.

That experience shaped my research instincts permanently. In hardware, an algorithm that cannot meet its area, latency, and precision budget is not a solution, however elegant its derivation. Error is not an abstraction but a quantity to be located, bounded, and justified. When I later moved into deep learning, I carried these habits across — and they turned out to be directly relevant rather than merely formative. Whole-slide pathology images are gigapixel-scale objects that must be tiled, sampled, and processed under severe memory and throughput constraints. The distinction between a model that runs comfortably on a well-provisioned GPU cluster and one that can run inside a Pakistani pathology laboratory is, in the end, a question of resource budgets of exactly the kind I spent my early career negotiating.

## 3. Machine Learning for Signal and Image Analysis

My research interest can be summarised as **machine learning for signal processing**, with biomedical images as the signal of primary interest. The move from one-dimensional signals to two-dimensional histopathology images was an extension rather than a break. Both are problems of recovering structured, decision-relevant information from high-dimensional measurements corrupted by acquisition variability — in one case by quantisation noise, jitter, and channel effects, and in the other by staining protocol, section thickness, scanner optics, and fixation artefact. The vocabulary changes; the underlying discipline of separating signal from nuisance variation does not.

My doctoral research (UMT, 2024) addressed **histopathology image analysis for the detection and staging of prostatic carcinoma**. Prostate cancer grading is a task in which inter-observer variability among expert pathologists is well documented, and in which a reproducible computational second reader therefore has clear and immediate clinical value. A significant methodological contribution of that work was to treat patch-level Gleason assessment as a **multi-label** rather than a single-label problem. This reflects the underlying biology: a single tissue region may legitimately exhibit more than one Gleason pattern, and forcing a mutually exclusive label onto such a region discards information that is clinically meaningful and injects avoidable noise into training. This component was published in *PLOS ONE* (19(7): e0304847, 2024).

I am currently preparing the multi-class component of the thesis as a coordinated series of manuscripts. The first presents the grading method itself. The second is an audit of evaluation practice in the computational grading literature — how splits are constructed, how leakage arises, how performance is reported, and how much of the reported progress survives stricter protocols. The third examines morphological descriptors that can be computed independently of the grading pipeline, so that model outputs can be cross-checked against measurable tissue properties rather than accepted on the strength of a validation score alone.

## 4. Current Programme: A National Prostate Cancer Pathology Resource

I am Principal Investigator of a competitively awarded **HEC National Research Programme for Universities (NRPU) project (Award Ref. 143787-121, 2026–2028)**, conducted by UMT in partnership with King Edward Medical University and Mayo Hospital, Lahore. The project is deliberately structured around two deliverables, one of which is a data resource and one of which is a method.

**(a) An expert-annotated prostate cancer histopathology dataset — the first of its kind in Pakistan.** The publicly available datasets on which computational pathology has been built are overwhelmingly derived from North American and European cohorts. Models trained on them encounter domain shift when applied to local tissue preparation protocols, staining practice, scanner characteristics, biopsy sampling conventions, and patient populations, and that shift is rarely quantified because the data needed to quantify it does not exist. A nationally sourced, pathologist-annotated resource is therefore both a scientific necessity and a public good. The project is designed from the outset around ethical governance, rigorous de-identification, and clear institutional data custody; ethical approval was granted by the UMT Research Ethics and Safety Committee in February 2026. Building such a resource also means building the human infrastructure around it — annotation protocols, adjudication procedures for disagreement between readers, and quality control — which is itself a transferable contribution.

**(b) An AI-based diagnostic tool for Gleason grading and perineural invasion (PNI) detection.** PNI — the tracking of tumour cells along nerve sheaths — carries prognostic weight in much of the urological literature, yet it is laborious to identify and consequently under-reported in routine practice. Computationally it is a hard problem of exactly the kind I find compelling: a small, sparse, morphologically subtle target distributed across a gigapixel field, with severe class imbalance and a limited supply of positive examples. It sits at the meeting point of small-object detection, weak supervision, and probability calibration. It is also a setting in which an overconfident detector is worse than no detector at all, because a false negative in a screening-assistive role removes a finding from the pathologist's attention rather than merely failing to add one. Designing the operating point, and the interface through which findings are surfaced for review, is as much a part of the research as the architecture.

## 5. Methodological Commitments

Four concerns run through my current work and will continue to organise it.

**Evaluation integrity.** A substantial portion of reported performance in medical imaging is an artefact of patient-level leakage, optimistic data splitting, uncalibrated probabilities, and absent external validation. I regard the systematic auditing of these practices as a legitimate research contribution in its own right, not as housekeeping preliminary to the real work, and I am pursuing it deliberately. The same failure modes recur across modalities: my parallel work on leakage-controlled machine learning for variant pathogenicity prediction arose precisely because the circularity problems visible in imaging benchmarks have close analogues in computational genomics. Methods that are honest about what they have not been tested on are more useful to clinicians than methods that are not.

**Explainability grounded in morphology.** Attribution that a pathologist cannot map onto glandular architecture, stromal reaction, or nuclear features is of limited clinical use, whatever its mathematical properties. My work on explainable segmentation for colorectal lesions, and the interpretability components of the prostate programme, aim at explanations expressed in the vocabulary of the reporting pathologist, so that a disagreement between model and reader becomes a discussion about tissue rather than an unresolvable conflict of authority.

**Privacy-preserving and federated learning.** Clinical data rarely travels, and in most jurisdictions it should not have to. My ongoing work on federated learning for colorectal lesion detection addresses multi-institutional model development without centralising patient data — a practical prerequisite for any national-scale collaboration in Pakistan, where data-sharing agreements between institutions are difficult to negotiate and easy to breach.

**Multimodal integration.** Histopathology is one channel among several. I am extending my work toward the joint modelling of imaging with clinical and molecular variables, including through participation in international multimodal prostate cancer challenges, on the view that grading and prognosis are ultimately inference problems over all available evidence rather than over pixels alone.

## 6. Directions for the Next Five Years

- **Self-supervised and foundation-model pretraining on locally acquired slides**, with systematic benchmarking of cross-population, cross-laboratory, and cross-scanner generalisation. The open question I want to answer quantitatively is how much of a foundation model's advantage survives transfer to a population and a preparation protocol it never saw.
- **Generalising rare-finding detection.** PNI is one instance of a broader class: clinically important, spatially sparse, under-reported findings in surgical pathology. I intend to treat it as a template rather than a special case.
- **Prospective reader studies** with practising pathologists, measuring the assistive effect on reporting time, diagnostic confidence, and inter-observer agreement, rather than offline accuracy alone.
- **Extension to other cancers of high local burden**, particularly breast, oral, and colorectal carcinoma, reusing the annotation infrastructure and governance framework established under the current project.
- **Deployment pathway work** — model compression, efficient inference on low-cost hardware, and the quality-assurance and regulatory groundwork that digital pathology in Pakistan will eventually require. This is where my earliest training becomes directly useful again.

## 7. Collaboration, Supervision, and Capacity Building

I lead final-year and graduate research at UMT and serve as Final Year Project Convener in my department, and I regard research training as inseparable from research itself. The most durable output of a funded project in a developing research ecosystem is often the people it trains. Through the Global Scholars Network I am particularly interested in:

- **Co-supervision** of MS and PhD scholars jointly with international and diaspora experts in computational pathology, medical image analysis, and machine learning;
- **Collaborative research and joint publication**, including shared benchmarks, reproducibility studies, and multi-site validation of methods developed in either direction;
- **Curriculum and faculty development** in medical imaging, deep learning, and research methodology, an area where structured external input has disproportionate effect;
- **Guest lectures, workshops, and doctoral training** on computational pathology and on rigorous evaluation practice in clinical machine learning.

What I bring to such collaborations is an active, competitively funded research programme with ethical clearance in place; a working clinical partnership with a major public-sector teaching hospital; access to locally sourced, expert-annotated pathology data under proper governance; and an engineering group capable of building, training, and validating systems end to end. What I seek in return is methodological depth — in foundation models, federated learning, clinical validation design, and biostatistics — together with the sustained international engagement that turns a national dataset into globally useful science and a local research group into a contributing member of an international field.

## 8. Areas of Expertise

Computational pathology, whole-slide image analysis, deep learning for medical imaging, prostate cancer grading and perineural invasion detection, explainable AI, federated and privacy-preserving learning, small-object detection, multimodal clinical modelling, machine learning for signal processing, VLSI implementation of DSP algorithms, direct digital frequency synthesis, Python, PyTorch, and reproducible research pipelines.
